excerpts.text: The **SI base units** are the standard [units of measurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Units_of_measurement "Units of measurement") defined by the [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units "International System of Units") (SI) for the seven [base quantities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_quantities "Base quantities") of what is now known as the [International System of Quantities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Quantities "International System of Quantities"): they are notably a basic set from which all other [SI units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_units "SI units") can be [derived](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_derived_unit "SI derived unit"). The units and their physical quantities are the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second "Second") for [time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time "Time"), the [metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter "Meter") for measurement of [length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length "Length"), the [kilogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram") for [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass "Mass"), the [ampere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampere "Ampere") for [electric current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_current "Electric current"), the [kelvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin") for [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature "Temperature"), the [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)") for [amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance"), and the [candela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candela "Candela") for [luminous intensity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminous_intensity "Luminous intensity").

excerpts.text: On 20 May 2019, as the final act of the [2019 redefinition of the SI base units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_redefinition_of_the_SI_base_units "2019 redefinition of the SI base units"), the [BIPM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Bureau_of_Weights_and_Measures "International Bureau of Weights and Measures") officially introduced the following new definitions, replacing the [preceding definitions of the SI base units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005-2019_definitions_of_the_SI_base_units "2005-2019 definitions of the SI base units").

| [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)") | mol | [amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance") | "The mole, symbol mol, is the SI unit of [amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance"). One mole contains exactly 6.022 140 76 × 1023 elementary entities. This number is the fixed numerical value of the [Avogadro constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avogadro_constant "Avogadro constant"), *N*A, when expressed in the unit mol−1 and is called the [Avogadro number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avogadro_number "Avogadro number"). The amount of substance, symbol *n*, of a system is a measure of the number of specified elementary entities. An elementary entity may be an atom, a molecule, an ion, an electron, any other particle or specified group of particles."[[1]](#cite_note-SI_9th_edition-1) | [Atomic weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_weight "Atomic weight") or [molecular weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_weight "Molecular weight") divided by the [molar mass constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_mass_constant "Molar mass constant"), 1 g/mol. | N |

excerpts.text: In 2019, four of the seven [SI base units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_base_unit "SI base unit") specified in the [International System of Quantities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Quantities "International System of Quantities") were redefined in terms of natural physical constants, rather than human artefacts such as the [International Prototype of the Kilogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Prototype_of_the_Kilogram "International Prototype of the Kilogram").[[1]](#cite_note-SI-statement-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Effective 20 May 2019, the 144th anniversary of the [Metre Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_Convention "Metre Convention"), the [kilogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram"), [ampere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampere "Ampere"), [kelvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin"), and [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)") are defined by setting exact numerical values, when expressed in SI units, for the [Planck constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planck_constant "Planck constant") (*h*), the [elementary electric charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_electric_charge "Elementary electric charge") (*e*), the [Boltzmann constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann_constant "Boltzmann constant") (*k*B), and the [Avogadro constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avogadro_constant "Avogadro constant") (*N*A), respectively.

* **Previous definition**: The mole is the [amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance") of a system that contains as many elementary entities as there are [atoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom "Atom") in 0.012 kilogram of [carbon-12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon-12 "Carbon-12"). When the mole is used, the elementary entities must be specified and may be atoms, [molecules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecule "Molecule"), [ions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion "Ion"), [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron"), other particles, or specified groups of such particles.

excerpts.text:
The revised definition breaks that link by making a mole a specific number of entities of the substance in question.

* **Previous definition:** The mole is the [amount of substance](/wiki/Physics:Amount_of_substance "Physics:Amount of substance") of a system that contains as many elementary entities as there are [atoms](/wiki/Physics:Atom "Physics:Atom") in 0.012 kilogram of [carbon-12](/wiki/Physics:Carbon-12 "Physics:Carbon-12"). When the mole is used, the elementary entities must be specified and may be atoms, [molecules](/wiki/Physics:Molecule "Physics:Molecule"), [ions](/wiki/Physics:Ion "Physics:Ion"), [electrons](/wiki/Physics:Electron "Physics:Electron"), other particles, or specified groups of such particles.
* **2019 definition:**[[7]](#cite_note-cipm_106-7): 22 The mole, symbol mol, is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076×1023 elementary entities. This number is the fixed numerical value of the [Avogadro constant](/wiki/Physics:Avogadro_constant "Physics:Avogadro constant"), *N*A, when expressed in the unit mol−1 and is called the Avogadro number.[[7]](#cite_note-cipm_106-7)[[48]](#cite_note-55) The amount of substance, symbol *n*, of a system is a measure of the number of specified elementary entities. An elementary entity may be an atom, a molecule, an ion, an electron, any other particle or specified group of particles.
